info.title: FOOTBALL OS API
info.description:
**FOOTBALL OS** — The Operating System for Football.

M0 foundation + M1 vertical slice: My Football (player identity) → Training Academy →
explainable progression → AI Coach → progress → history.

Data provenance: the training catalogue and any world data are **synthetic demo data**
and are labelled as such. AI surfaces run in **DEMO MODE** unless a provider key is
configured, and always say so.

schema.title: Response Healthz Api V1 Healthz Get

get.description:
Which milestones are live — the UI uses this instead of guessing.

M3 reports what the database actually holds rather than what the code could serve: the flag
flips to true only once the synthetic world is present in full, because a half-written world
must not be rendered as if it were real (spec §65, `DATA_POLICY.md`). `locales` likewise lists
only the language the UI ships today; §81 translations are `locales_planned`.

schema.title: Response Analyse Clip Api V1 Video  Ident  Analyse Post

get.description:
The clip itself, to its owner only — the browser needs it to show what was analysed.

A `<video>` element asks for byte ranges, and a server that cannot answer them makes the player
download the whole file before it can seek. So this route reads only the slice it was asked for,
and never the whole clip into memory.
One sampled frame as PNG, from the same set the measurements came from.
The bookkeeping for this clip's runs, so a report can be traced to the job that made it.

post.description:
Play the career's next round with the engine, then re-derive everything the page shows.

A career opened from a live challenge stops here once its window is used. That is the scenario
working, not a failure, so it answers `window_closed` with the rounds that closed it rather than a
generic refusal — and the run's own view is beside it, so the page can show the final verdict
instead of an error with nothing to read.

get.description:
Play the stored match again from its stored inputs and report whether it came out the same.

This is what spec §19 asks of a simulation: not that it is accurate, but that it is honest about
being a model and reproducible in its own terms. If the engine ever changes without its version
number moving, this is the check that stops matching.

get.description:
The vocabulary and the arithmetic: what a sentence may say, and what each saying does to the pool.

The integrity block is published rather than kept in a test because it is the part a reader has to trust:
the vocabulary agreeing with itself, the search answering every requirement kind the parser emits, a
report building over the stored pool that answers every field §24 lists with a figure that recomputes
from the attributes printed beside it, and a comparison whose every dimension is the leader its own
measures give it.

schema.title: Response Read Rules Api V1 Scout Rules Get

post.description: Read a scout's sentence without searching: what would be filtered, what was refused, what was ignored.

schema.title: Response Parse Api V1 Scout Parse Post

post.description: Search the stored world with a sentence, stated fields, or both, optionally judged against a career.

schema.title: Response Run Search Api V1 Scout Search Post

post.description:
§24's structured report for one stored player: thirteen fields, each one arithmetic over that row.

A career is optional, and its absence stays visible in the payload rather than being papered over:
`team_fit` is null and the risk list simply carries one factor fewer. A comparison behaves the same way —
§24 lists `Comparison`, and answering that field with nobody beside it would be a line that looks
measured and is not. The player is looked up before the role, so a wrong slug and a wrong role produce
the one refusal that is about the world rather than the one that is about this project's vocabulary.

schema.title: Response Read Report Api V1 Scout Report Post

post.description:
§27's ten dimensions for a pair of stored players, with no figure in the answer that ranks them as a whole.

The route is deliberately narrower than the report: no career, no role, no round. Each of those is a way
of judging one player against a context, and §27 asks for a comparison of two players instead — the
moment a context is allowed in, the payload starts carrying a figure that is about a club rather than
about the pair, which is the report's job. Both sides are looked up before anything is computed, and the
left is answered first when neither exists, so a typo says which half of the request it was.

schema.title: Response Rename Shortlist Api V1 Scout Shortlists  Ident  Patch

schema.title: Response Take Off List Api V1 Scout Shortlists  Ident  Items  Player  Delete

post.description:
M7's transfer simulation: what would be different if this career signed this player.

Read-only by design. §22's `POST /transfers/{career}/buy` is the door that moves a player, charges the budget
and writes a move row; this route calls none of it. It prices the player from the valuation of his stored row,
rebuilds the career's side with and without him through the selector the engine plays, and replays the next few
fixtures at the same seeds — so the only difference between the two scorelines is the eleven.

schema.title: Response Simulate A Transfer Api V1 Scout Simulate Transfer Post

CompareIn.title: CompareIn
CompareIn.description: §27's pair. Both sides are required: a comparison of one player is the refusal, not an empty answer.

OrganizationIn.title: OrganizationIn
OrganizationIn.description:
A tenant's identity. The slug is derived from the name here and never accepted from a caller.

`max_length` here is a body guard, not the rule: the published cap is `rules()["name_max"]`, and the
service answers an over-long name with `name_required` *and the two figures* (`length`, `max`) that a
page needs to show why. A request validator one character earlier would answer with a schema error that
carries neither, so the guard sits well above the cap the API advertises.

ReportIn.title: ReportIn
ReportIn.description: One player, optionally judged for a role and against one career, optionally measured beside another.

SearchIn.title: SearchIn
SearchIn.description: A sentence, stated fields, or both. Where both speak, both cuts apply and the response says so.

ShortlistIn.title: ShortlistIn
ShortlistIn.description:
§23's list: a name, the sentence it was built from, and the two links a read needs.

No figure belongs here. A list carries words and links; the players' numbers come back on every read from
the stored rows, which is what lets a list go stale about its own question instead of lying about a player.

The length caps are deliberately not pydantic constraints. A transport-level 422 names a field and a rule;
the service's refusal names the length it was handed and the limit it tripped over, which is the answer a
reader can check their own request against. So the cap lives in one place, and it is the service's.

ShortlistItemIn.title: ShortlistItemIn
ShortlistItemIn.description:
Which player, and the manager's own words about him — the note is the only other thing stored, and the
service is the one that says how long a note may be.

ShortlistPatchIn.title: ShortlistPatchIn
ShortlistPatchIn.description: The same four fields, all optional: a list can be renamed, re-questioned, or re-pointed at a career.

StartIn.title: StartIn
StartIn.description: What a caller may choose. The window, the budget, the objectives and the philosophy are not here.

TransferSimIn.title: TransferSimIn
TransferSimIn.description:
A career, a player, and how many future fixtures to look at.

`rounds` carries no pydantic bound on purpose: a transport 422 would name a field and a rule, while the
service's own refusal names the number it was handed and the window it falls outside of — and the cap exists
because reading too far ahead would quietly assume a squad that has since moved on, which is worth saying.
